transcript.text: Bosch integrated dishwasher showing E:15 and the pump keeps running. Model SMV4HTX31E. I've turned it off and on, still there

E:15 means the anti-flood protection has operated: water has reached the base tray, so the dishwasher deliberately keeps the drain pump running. Turning it off and on will not clear it while the base remains wet. Switch it off, unplug it and close the water tap, then check the door seal and spray arms as above. If those look sound, it is likely an internal leak and an engineer will need to locate and repair it; simply drying the base may make it run briefly but is not a repair.

I've already unplugged it for 24h and it ran one cycle then E:15 came back. The door seal looks okay and the filter is fairly clean. It's fitted under the worktop with a glued plinth so I can't pull it out or tilt it. Is there anything else I can check from the front?

Yes. The most useful check you can do from the front is the spray arms: with the dishwasher switched off and unplugged, pull out the racks and turn each arm by hand. Look closely along the seams and ends for a split, and check that no tall item or utensil could have stopped an arm or deflected its spray towards the bottom of the door. A split spray arm can leak only while washing, which fits it completing a cycle after drying out then returning to E:15.
ok, I'll check the spray arms. Anything else I should look at while I'm in there? I can see a little shine of water in the base tray through a gap by the plinth, if that helps.

Yes. Since water is visible in the base and E:15 returned after a full cycle, there is a genuine recurring leak rather than just a reset issue. While checking the spray arms, inspect the seams and end caps for a hairline split, clear any blocked jets, and make sure no tall plate, utensil or item hanging below the lower rack can stop an arm or aim spray at the bottom of the door. Also note whether there is unusual foam in the tub; washing-up liquid or too much detergent can force foam into the base tray. If the arms and loading are all sound, the remaining most likely cause is an internal leak such as a sump hose, pump seal or internal hose, which needs an engineer because the machine cannot be pulled out for safe access.
ok, I'll go through the spray arms and loading. I use tablets so there's no foam. If the arms look fine, I guess I need an engineer then?

Yes—if both spray arms are intact, clear and free to turn, and the loading is not interfering with them, an engineer is the sensible next step. The return of E:15 after one cycle, together with visible water in the base tray, points to a recurring leak rather than an electrical reset problem; an internal sump hose, pump seal or hose is then most likely. Before booking, the one worthwhile check that may avoid an appliance repair is the accessible hose connections under the sink: with the dishwasher switched off, unplugged and its water tap closed, look for dampness, drip trails, a loose fitting or a split at the inlet and drain hoses. If those are dry and the spray arms look sound, keep the water tap closed and arrange an engineer—the machine needs to be pulled out to trace the internal leak safely.
ok, I'll check the hoses under the sink too. The socket is in the adjacent cupboard behind the unit, so I'll unplug it from there. If it's all dry I'll book an engineer.

That is the right approach. With it unplugged at the adjacent-cupboard socket and the dishwasher water tap closed, put a dry sheet of kitchen roll around each accessible inlet and drain-hose joint under the sink; it shows even a slow seep more clearly than a visual look. Check for dampness, white water marks, a loose nut/clip or a split hose, but do not disturb any connection that is tight and dry. If both connections are dry and the spray arms/loading check out, keep the water supply off and book an engineer: the repeated E:15 and water in the base then make an internal leak the leading cause.
